Meanwhile, NetShield blocks known ad, tracking, and malware domains, helping prevent some unwanted resources from loading without guaranteeing ad-free streaming or protection against every threat. title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

title: This New iOS 27 Feature May Save You From Getting Scammed
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: LuckyDuck via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Starting with iOS 27, your iPhone now has a built-in scam prevention feature, designed to protect you from social engineering scams. These scams rely on pressure tactics to trick you into bypassing security features for your phone, laptop, or online accounts. Here's how iOS 27's "Impersonation Risk Detection" works, what it can do, and its current limitations.How Impersonation Risk Detection works to protect you from scamsIn a social engineering scam, a bad actor impersonates an official rep of a bank, government agency, or a tech company such as Apple, Google, or Microsoft. The scammer may even impersonate your friends, family members, or colleagues you trust. They'll try to force you to disable account security measures such as two-factor authentication, or talk you into sharing your financial information. They'll create a fake problem, establish trust, and then pressure you into making large payments. Apple says Impersonation Risk Detection can analyze information about your iPhone or iPad, your Apple Account, and check for signs of an active scam. Once it completes the analysis, iOS 27 will share a risk level with the app that's being targeted by scammers. Apple emphasizes that the app doesn't receive any data associated with your device or Apple Account that was used to assess the risk level.
From there, it's up to the app to decide how to proceed. If an app supports Impersonation Risk Detection, it may add a delay to each step you're trying to execute, show warnings, or even ask you to verify your identity. Apps can use various factors to decide if they need a risk assessment from iOS 27, which include big changes to your account, resetting its password, disabling two-factor authentication, making large payments, etc.What are the various risk levels in Impersonation Risk Detection?Once an app requests iOS 27 for a risk assessment, the operating system can conduct an analysis and place the action into one of three risk level markers (again, Apple doesn't control what apps do with the risk level information):Unknown: This means that iOS 27 couldn't detect any suspicious activity. Apple says that doesn't mean the action was confirmed as safe.Medium: This risk level is assigned when iOS 27 detects some signs of suspicious activity.High: This risk level is associated with significant signs of suspicious activity.How to enable Impersonation Risk Detection
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Once you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27 (or your iPad to iPadOS 27), go to Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and tap Impersonation Risk Detection. Enable the toggle next to "Share with App Developers." Now, tap Share with App Developers in the pop-up. Once Impersonation Risk Detection is enabled, you don't need to take further action. Note that when you try to disable this feature, it may take up to 24 hours to take effect. This is to protect you from scammers, who may pressure you into disabling the feature.In the same settings page, you'll be able to see which app requested access to your risk levels, and why. This will show up under the "Recent Activity" section. You'll also be able to turn off this feature for individual apps that appear in this section, but, again, it may take up to 24 hours to disable the setting.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The limitations of Impersonation Risk DetectionSecurity features are only as strong as their weakest links. In the case of iOS 27's Impersonation Risk Detection, there are two main weak links. First, this feature is disabled by default. Most people aren't going to dig deep enough into settings to discover it accidentally, and the feature isn't going to be used widely unless people know about it. Second, this feature also depends on app developers adding support for it. Big tech companies and indie developers may adopt it reasonably quickly, but other developers may not rush to implement this feature.There's also the fact that plenty of apps have already spent a lot of resources building up their own security infrastructure, and they may not necessarily see value in adding support for this feature. Here in India, all banking and payment apps show multiple full-screen warnings when you try to make a payment while on a phone call. Some apps may even disable payment features if they detect that a screen-sharing app is installed on your device. So, really, it will come down to how app developers respond to this feature.Does Impersonation Risk Detection keep my data private?Apple says that Impersonation Risk Detection performs its analysis on-device, and that the data used to generate the risk level doesn't leave your device. The company also highlights that the contents of your email, photos, or messages are not analyzed for the risk assessment. When an app requests a risk assessment, Apple claims it only receives information about the type of action you performed in that specific app. Once the risk level is generated, apps don't receive any additional data about you.

Open box usually means the packaging has been handled or returned, but the unit itself has been checked and works like new. This model plugs straight into a wall outlet and keeps the top socket usable, so it doesn’t block access in tight spaces. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost. A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself. Google: 15GB of free cloud storageThe most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number. 
Apple iCloud: 5GB of free cloud storageiCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month. Microsoft OneDrive: 5GB of free cloud storageSimilar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment. Box: 10GB of free cloud storageBox offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents. Dropbox: 2GB of free cloud storageDropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps. Proton Drive: 5GB of free cloud storageProton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MEGA: 20GB of free cloud storageMEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media. Other cloud storage services: Free storage amounts varyThere are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services. Password managers often include free storageYour password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB. How to organize and maximize your free storage spaceIf you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box. Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

title: Over 150 Million Driver's Licenses Have Been Leaked
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 11, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Yeong-Ung Yang/Newsday via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            If you have a driver's license in the U.S or Canada, there's a pretty good chance that your data was stolen.
                                            A massive hack at ID verification company IDScan.net compromised records for more than 150 million drivers.
                                            Be on the lookout for a notice from IDScan.net.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you have a driver's license in the U.S or Canada, there's a pretty good chance that your data was recently for sale on the dark web. A massive hack at ID verification company IDScan.net compromised records for more than 150 million drivers, resulting in scans of licenses being made available to bad actors. IDScan.net is a Louisiana-based company that provides identity and age verification services for industries ranging from casinos and cannabis dispensaries to hotels and car rentals. What happened with the IDScan.net breach?According to an incident notice on IDScan's website, the company received information "on or around" Sept. 1 that an unauthorized third party was able to gain access to stored customer data, including full names along with driver's license and government-issued ID numbers. This was around the time that a major breach was reported by cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs, who received a tip that driver's license information—including digital scans—was available for sale on the dark web via an identity theft service dubbed Nexus. The platform advertised access to more than 153 million driver's licenses, and Krebs and security researcher Zach Edwards verified the data and identified IDScan as the likely source. As TechCrunch reports, the FBI is investigating the breach, and the database has since been taken offline. 
What to do if your drivers license has been compromisedA lost or stolen driver's license creates a high risk of identity theft and fraud, as hackers can use it to open financial accounts and take out loans in your name, commit mail fraud, create a fake ID, and even develop a synthetic identity (which combines both real and fake personal data) that could be used to commit a crime. If thieves have access to your physical license or a scan, as in this latest breach, they have a complete set of information, including your birth date and photo, to assume your identity. Fraudsters can also do a lot of damage with just your driver's license number. If your driver's license information has been compromised in a breach, you should take all the usual steps against identity theft, including pulling your credit reports, monitoring your financial accounts, and setting up fraud alerts. (At this point in the data breach game, your credit should already be frozen unless you are actively applying for a new card or loan, but if you haven't yet, do it immediately.) 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Because your driver's license is so valuable to identity thieves, Experian also recommends requesting your driving record, which you can get from your state's department of motor vehicles, and running a background check on yourself. Both can reveal if any fraudulent activities have been carried out in your name—for example, if someone has been pulled over or if there are arrest warrants or criminal charges linked to your identity. You can file a police report for a lost or stolen license and report identity theft if you believe your information is being used fraudulently. IDScan.net is reportedly alerting individuals affected by this latest breach, and given its scale, you should be on the lookout for a notice. The company is offering credit monitoring and identity protection services to those impacted, and you can call 1-833-516-2980 to enroll.

title: These Are the Best Digital Subscriptions of 2026
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: visualspace / E+ via Getty Image
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're like me, you are paying for a ton of subscriptions you don't even remember signing up for. Let's make this the year of only having subscriptions that add to our lives. The digital services below are the best things you can subscribe to in 2026 if you want to actually improve yourself and your world, whether it's through cutting your DoorDash bill, supporting your local bookstore, or finding obscure movies to impress your friends. Best overall digital subscription of 2026: Apple One While there's no single digital service that everyone will like, Apple One comes close. Anyone with an iPhone (i.e., most phone users in the U.S.) will appreciate a single digital bundle that covers Apple Music, Apple TV+, Arcade, and extra iCloud storage. That's streaming, gaming, and storage covered for $21.95 a month. Pro tip: The Family Plan includes six separate accounts for $27.95 a month, and your "family" could include anyone, so get some friends together to get the most out of Apple. Best meal box service of 2026: Cook UnityI've never understood meal boxes that deliver ingredients and instructions. If I wanted to cook, I wouldn't be eating food out of a delivery box. Cook Unity gets it. The pitch is restaurant-quality meals created by star chefs like Esther Choi and Marcus Samuelsson for around $11 each, and the only "cooking" required is a little microwaving. If nothing else, this will save you a ton on DoorDash for those nights where you can't be bothered to make dinner. 
If you want to stay informed without doom-scrolling, and you want good recipes and better puzzles to boot, subscribe to the New York Times. An all-access subscription gives you access to the full New York Times archive (back to 1851!), NYT Cooking, daily crosswords, Wordle, Connections, Spelling Bee, and the 10,000-puzzle archive. The best gift box of 2026: Bespoke PostThere are gift box services for all kinds of specific niches, but Bespoke Post casts a wider net by letting users choose what comes in their box every month. It's heavily coded "man," but that's like half of everyone. One month, you can get high-end coffee supplies. The next, outdoor gear. If nothing catches your eye, you can just skip that month. If you want to open a present every month, all year, a subscription to Bespoke Post is for you. The best education subscription of 2026: MasterclassIf you want to make your brain smarter, a subscription to Masterclass is way cheaper than grad school. This educational streaming service covers a wide range of subjects from Science to Acting to Business, and it includes extensive lectures from heavyweights in each field. If you want to learn how to make films, you can take a deep dive with Martin Scorsese, or take a music lessons from Timbaland or cooking lessons from Gordon Ramsay. A subscription unlocks the entire library, so you can learn as much or as little as you choose. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The best entertainment subscription of 2026: Eternal FamilyI'm going way into left field with this choice, but I bet you already know that you can stream NBC content on Peacock and what's on Apple TV+. I bet you don't know about Eternal Family, a streaming service that bills itself as the "hidden gem video store." They don't mean "hidden gems" that are actually widely known like The Prestige or something. This is the uncut stuff, like Heino Pars' achingly beautiful 1983 stop motion film City of the Honey Makers (way better than The Bee Movie) or In the Dust of the Stars, a visionary science fiction film made behind the Iron Curtain in Romania in 1976. Every choice is a different strange delight. The best audiobook subscription of 2026: Libro.fmLibro.fm lets you listen to audiobooks while supporting your local independent bookstore instead of supporting a huge corporation that rhymes with "Schamazon." Libro's content is free of the Digital Rights Management of its main competitor, so you can listen to the books you buy however you like instead of locking yourself into a proprietary player. Libro's firm anti-AI narration stance ensures you won't be paying for robots to tell you bedtime stories, and you can choose which independent bookstore to support with Libro's profit-sharing model. Best outdoors/fitness subscription of 2026: AllTrailsWhen it comes to fitness subscriptions, services tend to focus on how you work out by letting you compare your workout to other people's or keep track of exactly how many calories you burn. AllTrails reminds you why you work out in the first place. Its focus is on the discovery and exploration of the natural wonders around you. A premium subscription unlocks tools to discover beautiful trails and navigate them safely, like offline maps, terrain previews, and more, so you can get out of the gym and into the world.

title: 10 Keyboard Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
body:
Khamosh Pathak
                            
        
            Khamosh Pathak
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceKhamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images/Apple
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        On the surface, the iPhone keyboard looks like it did a decade ago, but underneath, much has changed. In addition to the hidden features that have existed for years, Apple has slowly added features and gestures that make typing a bit easier. If you're still shaking your iPhone to undo text, it's time to dig deeper. These 10 hacks can help you make the most of typing on your iPhone. Use keyboard haptics to simulate a physical keyboardTyping on an iPhone’s glass surface can feel a bit lifeless, especially if you’re used to typing on mechanical keyboards on your Mac. While there’s no way to get a physical keyboard on the iPhone (unless you get something like the Clicks keyboard), you can simulate it. The iPhone has a built-in Taptic engine, which provides subtle vibrations as you interact with the device. While most know it from notifications, calls, and scrolling through various iOS UI elements, it can be enabled for the keyboard too. Go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Keyboard Feedback and enable \"Haptic Feedback." Use this hidden gesture to type one number from the main keyboardWhen you type on the iPhone keyboard, all you see are letters. To type numbers or symbols, you have to switch to the “123” keyboard layout instead—unless you use this hidden gesture, that is. See, each letter is already hiding a number or alternative symbol behind it. All you need to do to reveal it is to swipe from the 123 key. Once you do that, the keyboard will reveal numbers and symbols. Drag your finger to the number you want to enter, let go, and it’s done. The keyboard goes back to being a keyboard.
Use this camera trick to scan text into any field
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Apple
                    
    
The iPhone has OCR (optical character recognition) built into iOS. You use this anytime you copy text from an image in the Photos app. The same feature is integrated into the Camera app, and lets you paste that text straight into any field, bypassing the keyboard entirely. To do so, point the camera towards any text, and the app will frame it in a yellow border. You’ll also see a Live Text button in the bottom-right corner. Tap on it, select the text, and tap the Copy button. Now, open any text field, and you’ll see a suggestion to paste the text you just copied. Enable one-handed mode to shift the keyboard toward your thumb
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
If you have a large iPhone, typing with one hand can be extremely difficult. Instead, use the keyboard's one-handed mode. Tap and hold the Globe key to find options to dock the one-handed keyboard to the left or the right (below the list of all available keyboards). If you don’t see it, go to Settings > General > Keyboard > One-Handed Keyboard and choose Left or Right from here. Once enabled, you’ll see a shrunken keyboard layout docked to one side of the screen. Tap the Arrow button to change the docking position. Unfortunately, unlike Gboard on Android, you can’t resize the keyboard itself, but this does make it much easier to use your keyboard with one hand. Build a text replacement library for the phrases you retype dailyApple’s built-in Text Replacement feature can transform a couple of pre-programmed letters into canned responses. That could be your address, an email template for clients, a signature, a repeated sign-off message, anything you frequently type. Go to Settings > General > Keyboard > Text Replacement. Here, tap the Plus button from the top, add the expanded response in the "Phrase" field and the trigger characters in the "Shortcut" field. Double- and triple-tap to select a word, sentence, or paragraphYou can simply drag the iPhone’s cursor to select text. But instead of fiddling with the little cursor point, try tapping on the screen. You can double-tap a word to quickly select it; triple-tap, and you’ll select the sentence. Tap four times, and now the entire paragraph is selected. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use these gestures to master quick edits Once you’ve selected the text, pinch in with three fingers to quickly copy the text. Pinch outwards with three fingers to paste the text. You can also swipe left with three fingers to undo anything you just did. For precise text selection, nothing beats the trackpad hack. You might already know that if you press and hold the Space bar on the iPhone keyboard, the whole thing turns into a trackpad. But you can also use this feature to select text. Keep your finger on the Space bar, but use another finger to move the cursor to select the text. Reset your keyboard dictionary to improve suggestionsThere may be times when the iPhone keyboard goes haywire. Autocorrect might keep suggesting words you never type, or it keeps bringing up specific casual words you type in a group chat, but don’t mean to repeat. If you’re fed up with keyboard suggestions, there is an out. You can reset the whole thing, starting fresh by rebuilding the suggestions library. Go to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Reset > Reset Keyboard Dictionary to get started. Turn on multilingual support to type in two languages with the same keyboardIf you’re multilingual, you might constantly switch between keyboards to type in your target language. Now, you don't need to do that. You can enable multilingual support to type in different languages on a single keyboard. When you enable two languages, the iPhone keyboard adapts automatically. It knows which language you’re typing and will even provide different suggestions based on it. Go to Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards > Add New Keyboard. Choose a language, and then select if you want to add a new keyboard, or if you want to add the language to your existing keyboard. Use Writing Tools to proofread a message before you send itYou shouldn’t trust AI to write for you, but you can use it to proofread and edit text you’ve crafted yourself. And there’s no need to pay for an AI subscription either. If you have Apple Intelligence built into your iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro and later), you can use the Writing Tools feature instead. Writing Tools is integrated into the Notes app, Mail app, and basically anywhere you write text. Select the text, and from the pop-up menu, choose "Writing Tools." From here, ask Siri to make the text shorter, format it to make it sound more formal, and, of course, to check for grammar and spelling mistakes.
